title: Why You'd Never Survive a Giant Asteroid Impact
screen_title: Why You'd Never Survive an Asteroid Impact
subtitle: And how we're learning to stop one
yt_title: Why You'd Never Survive a Giant Asteroid Impact
intro: What would actually happen if a giant asteroid hit Earth? We look at the rocks that hit us every day, the Tunguska blast that flattened 80 million trees, the asteroid that ended the dinosaurs near Mexico, and the moment humans first pushed an asteroid off course. Could we stop the next one?
questions: Did you know dozens of tons of space dust fall on Earth every day?
Do you think we would spot a dangerous asteroid in time?
What should we never get close to next?
tags: what if an asteroid hit earth

segments.text: Sixty-six million years ago, a mountain-sized rock fell out of the sky. In a single day, the world changed forever. Could it happen again? And what would it be like to be there?

Welcome to Next Stop: Universe. If you enjoy calm, easy-to-follow journeys through space, tap subscribe. Today we find out why you'd never survive a giant asteroid impact, and how humans are learning to stop one.
Our solar system is full of leftover rubble from when the planets formed: asteroids, mostly orbiting between Mars and Jupiter.
segments.headline: Leftover rubble

segments.text: Some are huge. Vesta, one of the biggest, is over five hundred kilometers wide.
segments.headline: Vesta

segments.text: Some are piles of loose rubble, barely holding together, like the asteroid Bennu, visited by NASA's OSIRIS-REx spacecraft.
segments.headline: Bennu

segments.text: Others come in pairs, two rocks orbiting each other, like this one.
segments.headline: Double asteroids

segments.text: And some cross Earth's orbit. These are called near-Earth asteroids.
segments.headline: Near-Earth asteroids

segments.text: In fact, Earth gets hit every single day. Not by big rocks, but by dust and pebbles.
segments.headline: Every day

segments.text: Scientists estimate that dozens of tons of space material fall on Earth every day. Most of it as tiny dust.
When a small grain burns up in our atmosphere, we see a shooting star.
segments.headline: Shooting stars

segments.text: Bigger pieces sometimes survive and land as meteorites. This one, the Willamette meteorite, weighs over fifteen tons.

files: Willamette meteorite at Dorothy and Lewis B. Cullman Hall of the Universe.jpg
visual.query: Willamette meteorite at Dorothy and Lewis B. Cullman Hall of the Universe

segments.headline: Meteorites

segments.text: Some meteorites are older than the Earth itself. Holding one is like holding a piece of the birth of the solar system.
So here's my first question. Did you know that dozens of tons of space dust land on Earth every day? Tell us in the comments.

visual.q: Did you know dozens of tons of space dust fall on Earth every day?

segments.text: Sometimes, a bigger rock arrives. On the morning of February fifteenth, twenty thirteen, a space rock about twenty meters wide streaked over the city of Chelyabinsk, in Russia.
segments.headline: Chelyabinsk

segments.text: For a moment, it shone brighter than the Sun. Then it exploded high in the air, about thirty kilometers up.
segments.headline: Brighter than the Sun

segments.text: The shock wave arrived over a minute later. It shattered windows across the city, and around fifteen hundred people were injured, mostly by flying glass.
Many people had walked to their windows to look at the bright flash. That's why scientists now say: if you ever see a huge fireball, stay away from windows for a couple of minutes.
segments.headline: A life-saving tip

segments.text: But every century or so, something much bigger arrives. On June thirtieth, nineteen oh eight, a space rock exploded over Siberia, near the Tunguska river.
segments.headline: Tunguska

segments.text: It was probably only about fifty or sixty meters wide. It exploded in the air, several kilometers up.
The blast flattened around eighty million trees over more than two thousand square kilometers.
It was so remote that, as far as we know, no one was killed. If it had exploded over a city, it could have destroyed it.
segments.headline: If it hit a city

segments.text: Now let's imagine the real monster. Sixty-six million years ago, an asteroid about ten kilometers wide headed straight for Earth.
segments.headline: 10 km wide

segments.text: It was traveling at about twenty kilometers per second. It crossed our whole atmosphere in just a few seconds.

visual.label: impact speed
visual.sub: through the atmosphere in a few seconds

segments.text: It hit near what is now the Yucatán Peninsula, in Mexico, and left a crater about one hundred eighty kilometers wide, now buried underground.
segments.headline: Yucatán, Mexico

segments.text: The energy released was billions of times greater than the bomb dropped on Hiroshima.
What would it have been like to be there? If you stood within hundreds of kilometers, the fireball would reach you first. Then the blast wave, then a rain of molten rock falling from the sky.
segments.headline: The first minutes

segments.text: Along the coasts, giant tsunamis swept inland. Earthquakes shook the whole planet.
segments.headline: Tsunamis

segments.text: And then, darkness. Dust and soot filled the sky. For months, maybe years, the Sun was dimmed, plants struggled, and the planet cooled.

files: ISS-20 Thunderstorms on the Brazilian Horizon.jpg
visual.query: ISS-20 Thunderstorms on the Brazilian Horizon

segments.headline: Darkness

segments.text: About three out of every four species on Earth disappeared, including all the big dinosaurs.
But small creatures survived. Among them were tiny mammals, our distant ancestors. And some dinosaurs survived too. We call them birds.
segments.headline: The survivors

segments.text: Here's my second question. Do you think we would spot a dangerous asteroid in time to stop it? Tell us in the comments.

visual.q: Do you think we'd spot a dangerous asteroid in time?

segments.text: So, are we in danger today? Astronomers watch the sky every night, searching for near-Earth asteroids.

files: 2018 Night Sky Festival- Stargazing in the Meadow (44025262174).jpg
visual.query: 2018 Night Sky Festival- Stargazing in the Meadow (44025262174)

segments.headline: Watching the sky

segments.text: More than thirty-five thousand near-Earth asteroids have been found so far.
The good news: astronomers believe they've found more than nine out of ten of the giant ones, a kilometer or bigger. None of them is on course to hit us in the next hundred years.
segments.headline: The giants are tracked

segments.text: The harder part is the smaller ones, the size of a stadium or a city block. Many of those are still out there, unseen.
Why do we miss them? Many approach from the direction of the Sun, where its glare hides them, just like Chelyabinsk did.
segments.headline: Hidden in the glare

segments.text: That's why NASA is building a new space telescope called NEO Surveyor. It will hunt for asteroids in infrared light, where even dark rocks glow with warmth.
segments.headline: NEO Surveyor

segments.text: Look at our Moon to see what we're dealing with. With no air and no weather to erase them, its craters record billions of years of impacts.

files: Earth, Moon and Lunar Module, AS11-44-6643.jpg
visual.query: Earth, Moon and Lunar Module, AS11-44-6643

segments.headline: The Moon remembers

segments.text: In early twenty twenty-five, a newly found asteroid, twenty twenty-four Y R four, briefly had about a three percent chance of hitting Earth in twenty thirty-two. More observations ruled that out.
segments.headline: A close call on paper

segments.text: And on April thirteenth, twenty twenty-nine, the asteroid Apophis will pass closer to Earth than some of our satellites. Millions of people will see it with their own eyes. But it will miss.
segments.headline: Apophis, 2029

segments.text: But what if one was coming? In twenty twenty-two, humans tried something for the very first time.
segments.headline: The DART mission

segments.text: NASA's DART spacecraft flew straight into a small asteroid called Dimorphos, which orbits a bigger one, Didymos.
segments.headline: Target: Dimorphos

segments.text: On September twenty-sixth, twenty twenty-two, it hit at about twenty-two thousand kilometers per hour.
The impact blasted out a huge trail of debris, like a comet's tail. Hubble even spotted boulders drifting away.

files: Twin Tail Revealed in New Hubble Image of Didymos-Dimorphos System Following DART Impact (opo22056a).jpg
visual.query: Twin Tail Revealed in New Hubble Image of Didymos-Dimorphos System Following DART Impact (opo22056a)

segments.headline: A tail of debris

segments.text: And it worked. Dimorphos's orbit got shorter by about thirty-two minutes. Humans had changed the path of a celestial body for the first time.
Europe's Hera spacecraft is on its way to inspect the crater up close, to learn exactly how hard we pushed.

files: Hubble sees boulders escaping from asteroid Dimorphos (heic2307a).jpg
visual.query: Hubble sees boulders escaping from asteroid Dimorphos (heic2307a)

segments.headline: Hera: the follow-up

segments.text: Asteroids aren't only dangerous. They may also have helped make life possible.
segments.headline: Not only dangerous

segments.text: Japan's Hayabusa two brought pieces of the asteroid Ryugu back to Earth in twenty twenty. NASA's OSIRIS-REx returned samples of Bennu in twenty twenty-three.
segments.headline: Samples brought home

segments.text: Inside the Bennu samples, scientists found amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, and all five of the bases used in DNA and RNA.
segments.headline: Building blocks of life

segments.text: So long ago, rocks from space may have delivered some of the ingredients of life to the young Earth. The same kind of rocks that, much later, ended the age of dinosaurs.

files: Earth, Moon and Lunar Module, AS11-44-6643.jpg
visual.query: Earth, Moon and Lunar Module, AS11-44-6643

segments.headline: Givers and takers

segments.text: So, would you survive a giant asteroid impact? Not if you were anywhere near it. But the most important lesson is this: for the first time in Earth's history, a species can see them coming.
segments.headline: The verdict

segments.text: The dinosaurs had no telescopes and no space program. We do. If we find a dangerous asteroid years in advance, a small push may be all it takes.
